question: In the light of the European Parliament resolution on the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘My Voice, My Choice’, which highlights that practical barriers to accessing safe abortion services persist in the European Union, a recent journalistic investigation in Greece has found that a significant number of public hospitals do not provide abortion services, even though abortion is allowed under Law 1609/1986 (Government Gazette, Series I, No 86/3-7-1986).

These services are not being provided due to conscientious objection by medical staff, coupled with the lack of a functioning referral mechanism, particularly in island and remote areas. This results in women travelling to other regions or turning to the private sector.

Given that the lack of effective access to a legal health service based on place of residence or financial wherewithal may constitute indirect discrimination and a gender equality issue, taking into account Articles 21, 23 and 35 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, as well as Article 168(1) TFEU and Principle 16 of the European Pillar of Social Rights, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it consider that extensive conscientious objection without effective alternative access is compatible with the obligation of equal access to health services?
What specific obligations do Member States have to ensure a functioning referral system in such cases?
Does the Commission intend to assess geographical disparities in access to legal abortion services within Member States?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.4.2026) Pursuant to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, EU action shall respect the responsibilities of the Member States for the definition of their health policy and for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care.
It is therefore for Member States to regulate the right of healthcare providers to object to providing certain healthcare services on ethical grounds.

As announced in the recently adopted Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030, in full respect of the Treaties, and in order to protect women’s health by supporting and complementing Member States’ health action regarding women’s access to sexual and reproductive health and rights, the Commission envisages to carry out a mapping of practices and international frameworks in this area.
It also plans to develop a framework and methodology for systemic data collection to improve the evidence base on sexual and reproductive health and rights1.
